fetched_contents.text: Unraveling the Mechanical Behavior of Softwood Secondary Cell Walls through Atomistic Simulations Abstract The plant cell wall (PCW) is a remarkable biomaterial, endowing plants with strength, stiffness, and defense against pathogens and chemical agents. This complex structure, mainly composed of cellulose in a matrix of hemicellulose, lignin, and water, exhibits impressive mechanical properties. However, the link between its molecular architecture and macroscopic mechanics is not fully understood. This study uses molecular dynamics simulations to examine the nanomechanical behavior of spruce wood’s S2 layer. Multicomponent models including cellulose, hemicellulose (xylan and mannan), lignin, and water were developed. Simulations showed that water acts as a “molecular lubricant”, mediating critical interactions between the components of the system. Tension and compression tests on the models displayed realistic mechanical behavior. Our results show that cellulose microfibrils bear the primary load, while lignin dissipates stress under compression. These findings offer new insights into the relationship between the molecular structure and mechanical function in this complex biomaterial. ---------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------- Introduction The plant cell wall (PCW) is a complex biomolecular structure crucial for plant growth, development, and mechanical stability, primarily composed of lignocellulosic biopolymers, including cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. PCW also incorporates ions, proteins, and minor organic compounds. This intricate structure provides vital support and chemical protection against physical stresses and pathogens. The PCW is typically subdivided into the middle lamella (ML), primary cell wall (CW1), and up to three secondary cell wall layers (S1, S2, and S3). Among these layers, the secondary cell wall, particularly rich in cellulose, plays a critical role in providing high mechanical stiffness and strength to plants. This is particularly evident in tall plants such as spruce, pine, oak, and birch, where the secondary cell wall can constitute up to 90% of the thickness of the PCW. The S2 layer, which comprises approximately 80% of the thickness of the secondary cell wall, is indispensable to ensure robust mechanical properties. Its unique architecture, resembling reinforced concrete, features cellulose fibrils embedded within a matrix of hemicellulose, lignin, and water. Plant species exhibit unique variations in the composition, spatial distribution, and interactions of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin within their cell walls, leading to distinct material properties. For example, while grasses and herbs exhibit a lignin content comparable to hardwoods (17–24 and 18–25%, respectively), − their lignin composition and lignin-cellulose interactions differ significantly from those of hardwoods. Softwoods are characterized by a higher abundance of mannan compared to xylan and possess highly hydrated lignin. , In contrast, hardwoods exhibit extensive lignin–lignin assemblies, increasing the hydrophobicity of the cell wall and indirectly promoting the association of 3-fold xylans with cellulose fibrils. These distinct structural features at the molecular level ultimately underpin the characteristic mechanical properties of softwoods (lightweight and flexible) and hardwoods (high density and stiffness). Hemicelluloses play a vital role in mediating lignin-cellulose interactions and even influencing fibril–fibril contacts. The carbohydrate decoration pattern significantly impacts these interactions, as demonstrated by Berglund and colleagues. They observed that mannan acts as an adhesive in bacterial cellulose, while xylan exhibits lubricating properties, reducing fibril adhesion. Furthermore, Penttilä et al. highlighted the role of hemicelluloses in influencing fibril packing and inducing a transition in cellulose from type Iα to Iβ, with xylan chains amplifying these effects. The even spacing of xylan decorations, while allowing for minor branching patterns, enables these hemicelluloses to interact effectively with both the hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces of cellulose. − In addition to hemicellulose, the distribution of water significantly influences the structural properties of the plant cell wall. , The water content plays a key role in determining the mechanical behavior of the cell wall. For instance, living, hydrated wood exhibits elasticity and recovers after deformation, whereas dried wood often fractures in a brittle manner. , Moreover, confined water within the cellulose microfibrils promotes fibril–fibril interactions. However, thermal pretreatments reduce the water content within these microfibrils, leading to fibril coalescence, increased cellulose crystallinity, and altered stress distribution. , Interestingly, dried softwoods can partially regain interfibril cellulose distances after rewetting. Nevertheless, some cellulose chains, previously in direct contact with water, become bound to hemicellulose, hindering subsequent water reentry. While water does not rehydrate the xylan-cellulose interface, it fully restores mannan-cellulose contacts, with a small fraction of mannan chains remaining mobile. Despite lignin’s inherent tendency toward self-aggregation, which increases hydrophobicity, softwood lignins exhibit a more dispersed distribution compared to their hardwood counterparts. Submission received: 18 September 2021 / Revised: 11 October 2021 / Accepted: 13 October 2021 / Published: 19 October 2021 Abstract This work examines the effect of thermal modification temperatures in the production of thermally modified wood on the cutting and fracture parameters when cutting heat-treated spruce wood by a circular sawblade machine. The samples were thermally modified at 160, 180, 200, and 220 °C. One sample was unmodified and was used as a reference sample. On the basis of the performed experiments, the fracture parameters (fracture toughness and shear yield strength) were calculated for the axial–perpendicular direction of cutting. In comparison with the theoretical assumptions, the influence of temperature on the cutting and fracture parameters was confirmed. Thermally treated wood is characterized by increased fragility and susceptibility to crack formation, as well as reduced density, bending strength, and shear strength. These properties significantly affect the size of the cutting force and feed force, as well as the fracture parameters. As the temperature increases, the values of these parameters decrease. The mentioned material characteristics could be useful for the optimization of the cutting process, as well as for the issue of energy consumption during the machining of heat-treated wood. 1. Introduction Wood has always been a material that humans use daily, and since it is an available renewable building material, there is a good chance that this will still be true in the future [1]. In civil engineering, wood is most often incorporated in timber structures and timber buildings [2]. Over the last twenty years, it has also been used for facades and terrace floors; however, its organic composition affects these uses rather negatively [3]. This is mainly due to the fact that untreated wood is subject to biological and weathering degradation, to which it is exposed when it is used as an unprotected exterior [4]. However, with advanced industrial methods, such as thermal modification, this situation has largely improved [5]. Since the beginning of the development of thermal modification, heat-treated timber has been a frequent subject of research investigations. Although this is one of many possible wood hydrothermal processing techniques, it is the most frequently used method after kiln drying [6]. By altering the wood structure, which varies depending on the temperature used [7], the thermally treated wood has properties different from those of untreated wood [8]. The most important change is the gradual breakdown of hemicelluloses and, partly, cellulose at the locations of its amorphous structure. This mainly results in a significant reduction in bending strength, with the modulus of elasticity in bending being disproportionately less reduced [9]. An interesting consequence, in terms of mechanical properties, is an increase in hardness [9,10], but this has not always been confirmed [8]. The reduction of density [11] and the esterification of cellulose mean that thermally treated wood has fewer free hydroxyl groups [12], leading to a rapid decrease in the equilibrium moisture content of the wood [13], which is, thus, less susceptible to biodegradation [14]. Changes in the mechanical properties strongly correlate with the increasing temperature used for the modification. Although the weakened thermally modified wood is not suitable for structural purposes [15], it is increasingly used in practice, for example, for facade paneling, terrace floors, and also various elements in the urban space, as its increased biological resistance finds its application there [16]. Unlike physical and mechanical properties, which are described very extensively in the literature, there is a lack of studies focused on the technological properties of heat-treated wood. However, changes in the mechanical and physical properties are reflected in the machining of thermally modified wood [17]. As the density of the thermally modified wood decreases, the cutting force is lowered during machining [18,19], which is also reflected in the reduction in energy consumption [20]. In the past, tests were conducted regarding the effect of thermal modification on the machining force, but they were mostly related to milling [18,21] or grinding [22]. On the other hand, the cutting process has not been given much attention in the area of thermally modified wood. Additionally, new findings have introduced a relatively new method to the machining process, which is based on the cutting-force determination using fracture mechanics. This method was first applied to homogeneous materials, in particular, to metal machining [23]. The method consists of the definition of the fracture toughness and the shear yield strength [24], i.e., unlike conventional methods of calculating the cutting force, this method is not based on the determination of the specific cutting resistance, kc [25], which is a function of many factors in the case of wood machining. The computational model also uses the application of the Ernst–Merchant theory in the conditions of sawblade timber cutting. The method was later applied to a wide range of materials [26], including wood [27,28,29,30,31], as it can take into account the effect of the altered material structure on the size of the cutting force. Wood-component interactions drive softening during veneer manufacturing because the cell wall is a multi-component matrix of cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and water, and each component responds differently to moisture, pressure, and thermal stress [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that wood cell walls are mainly composed of cellulose in a matrix of hemicellulose, lignin, and water, and that this structure exhibits impressive mechanical properties [N2-F2]. It also notes that water acts as a “molecular lubricant,” mediating critical interactions between the components of the system [N2-F2], and that tension and compression tests on multicomponent models displayed realistic mechanical behavior [N2-F2]. This means softening is not simply a property of one component alone, but an emergent behavior arising from how the components move, bond, and lubricate under processing conditions.

Moisture and pressure are central to softening in veneer processing because they alter the state of the cell wall. The evidence on veneer drying says veneer is dried in a drier circulating hot and humid air, with accurate dewpoint control being essential [N3-R3]. It also notes that steam at atmospheric pressure but temperatures higher than 212°F can be used to control moisture content in wood [N3-R4]. Another source explicitly says that high temperatures can achieve substantial densification despite moisture loss, while 90°C offers a more balanced approach [N3-R1]. This suggests moisture is a double-edged factor: it enables softening by keeping the cell wall pliable, but it also must be controlled carefully to avoid over-drying, which can damage mechanical properties [N3-R2]. The practical implication is that softening during veneer processing is especially sensitive to dewpoint control, steam temperature, and the moisture content trajectory through the drying cycle [N3-R3][N3-R4].

Cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin respond to thermal stress in different ways. The cell-wall context explains that cellulose microfibrils bear the primary load, while lignin dissipates stress under compression [N2-F2]. It also notes that thermal pretreatments reduce the water content within cellulose microfibrils, leading to fibril coalescence, increased cellulose crystallinity, and altered stress distribution [N2-F2]. Hemicelluloses are described as mediators of lignin–cellulose interactions and even influencing fibril–fibril contacts [N2-F2]. This means that thermal stress affects softening through several channels: it can crystallize cellulose, reduce water lubrication, change hemicellulose–lignin interactions, and alter how lignin dissipates stress [N2-F2]. In other words, softening is not just a simple temperature-dependent relaxation; it is a competition between stress relaxation, crystallization, and interaction changes.

The interaction mechanisms causing wood to soften during drying or pressing include water lubrication, stress redistribution, and weakening of interfacial bonds. The evidence states that water acts as a “molecular lubricant,” mediating critical interactions between the components of the system [N2-F2]. It also says that thermal pretreatments reduce water content within microfibrils, leading to fibril coalescence and altered stress distribution [N2-F2]. A separate source on wood working processes notes that when heat and moisture are applied, lignin softens temporarily, allowing the wood fibers to slide instead of breaking [N4-F3]. Another source says moisture makes wood more bendable, along with heat, and that lignin softening is central to this behavior [N4-R4]. Together, these mechanisms show that softening during veneer processing is driven by a combination of lubrication, stress redistribution, and temporary softening of lignin and other components [N2-F2][N4-F3][N4-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a picture in which veneer softening is caused by moisture enabling lubrication and temporary plasticity, pressure redistributing stress, and thermal stress altering cellulose crystallinity, hemicellulose interactions, and lignin behavior [N2-F2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-F3]. The practical result is that softening is a highly context-dependent process, sensitive to the exact combination of moisture, pressure, and temperature rather than a single factor alone [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-R4].

Lignin’s role in wood softening is determined by its chemical and structural features. The direct evidence on lignin’s glass transition temperature shows that lignin is a complex aromatic macromolecule with a Tg ranging from 90 to 150°C, depending on process conditions, extraction method, and source [N1-F1]. The same source also explains that lignin’s high Tg is largely associated with hydrogen bonding between phenolic hydroxyl groups and the higher quantity of aromatic rings in the main chain [N1-F1]. These features make lignin more rigid and thermally stable than many synthetic polymers, but they also mean that softening occurs only when thermal energy disrupts these bonds and the aromatic architecture [N1-F1]. The evidence further notes that lignin’s Tg lies between 100 and 180°C and that the values obtained in the study are higher than some literature values reported for kraft lignin, partly because of its more condensed structure [N1-F1]. This indicates that lignin’s Tg is not a fixed number but is sensitive to the lignin’s source and isolation method [N1-F1].

Near lignin’s Tg, thermal and mechanical changes in lignin-rich wood include temporary softening, stress redistribution, and a reduction in rigidity. The evidence on wood working processes states that when heat and moisture are applied, lignin softens temporarily, allowing wood fibers to slide instead of breaking [N4-F3]. It also notes that moisture makes wood more bendable, along with heat, and that lignin softening is central to this behavior [N4-R4]. A related source on lignin softening in woodworking processes provides a brief theoretical summary of the topic, though the excerpt provided does not give detailed mechanics beyond stating that lignin softening is relevant to woodworking at elevated temperatures [N4-R1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that near Tg, lignin-rich wood becomes more pliable because the aromatic matrix is temporarily relaxed rather than permanently degraded [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Lignin’s Tg compares with cellulose and hemicellulose behavior in a way that reflects the broader wood-component structure. The wood-cell-wall context notes that cellulose is generally responsible for mechanical properties, while lignin is responsible for thermal stability [N2-R4]. It also states that lignin decomposes in a wider temperature range (423–1173 K) than hemicellulose (493–588 K) and cellulose (588–673 K) [N2-R2]. This means that lignin’s degradation onset is later than hemicellulose and cellulose, but its thermal stability is not the only relevant factor for softening. The evidence also says that thermal pretreatments reduce water content within cellulose microfibrils, leading to fibril coalescence, increased cellulose crystallinity, and altered stress distribution [N2-F2]. This implies that softening is not just about lignin’s Tg; it is also about how lignin interacts with cellulose and hemicellulose under thermal stress [N2-R2][N2-F2].

Lignin softening differs from other wood-component transitions because it is more about temporary pliability than irreversible phase change. The evidence indicates that lignin’s Tg is associated with hydrogen bonding and aromatic structure, which are disrupted by heat and moisture, but this disruption is reversible or at least temporary [N1-F1][N4-F3]. In contrast, cellulose and hemicellulose also undergo thermal changes, but their decomposition ranges are narrower and more irreversible [N2-R2]. The wood-cell-wall context further explains that cellulose microfibrils bear the primary load, while lignin dissipates stress under compression [N2-F2]. This means that lignin’s role is more about stress dissipation and temporary plasticity, whereas cellulose’s role is more about load-bearing and crystallization [N2-F2]. Overall, lignin softening is distinct because it enables sliding rather than fracture, whereas other transitions may signal irreversible damage or structural collapse [N4-F3][N2-F2].

Softening in veneer manufacturing relates closely to practical processing conditions because moisture, temperature, and pressure are the main variables that control the cell wall’s state and the way wood responds to pressing. The evidence on veneer drying says veneer is dried in a drier circulating hot and humid air, and accurate dewpoint control is essential [N3-R3]. It also notes that steam at atmospheric pressure but temperatures higher than 212°F can be used to control moisture content in wood [N3-R4]. This shows that moisture is a primary driver of softening and must be managed carefully, because high temperatures can achieve substantial densification despite moisture loss, while lower temperatures may offer a more balanced approach [N3-R1]. The practical implication is that softening is especially sensitive to dewpoint and steam temperature, not just to the final moisture content [N3-R3][N3-R4].

Processing parameters most sensitive to wood-component transitions include temperature, moisture, and pressure. The evidence on veneer drying says that drying temperatures of 185°C/SD, 180°C/GD, and 240°C/GD negatively affected bending strength and modulus of elasticity [N3-R2]. Another source says that high temperatures can achieve substantial densification despite moisture loss, while 90°C offers a more balanced approach [N3-R1]. This indicates that temperature sensitivity is not uniform: high temperatures can densify wood, but they can also damage mechanical properties [N3-R2]. Pressure is also important because veneer pressing must keep the material together despite high temperature and pressure, and rays have thick, strong walls that help them stay together during pressing [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that thermal pretreatments reduce water content within cellulose microfibrils, leading to fibril coalescence, increased cellulose crystallinity, and altered stress distribution [N2-F2]. This means pressure sensitivity is compounded by thermal and moisture history, because the cell wall’s internal structure can change before pressing begins [N2-F2][N3-R2].

Softening affects veneer quality and bonding in several ways. First, the evidence suggests that softening enables plastic deformation rather than fracture, which can improve formability during pressing [N4-F3][N4-R4]. Second, the veneer-drying evidence shows that high drying temperatures can negatively affect bending strength and modulus of elasticity [N3-R2], which is directly relevant to veneer quality because lower strength and stiffness reduce the material’s ability to withstand subsequent processing steps. Third, the evidence on thermal modification notes that thermally treated wood is characterized by increased fragility and susceptibility to crack formation, as well as reduced density, bending strength, and shear strength [N5-F4]. This implies that softening during veneer processing can improve short-term formability, but may compromise long-term strength and dimensional stability [N3-R2][N5-F4]. Bonding is also affected because the evidence on wood working processes says that lignin softening temporarily allows wood fibers to slide rather than break [N4-F3]. This behavior is relevant to bonding because it may improve adhesion during pressing by reducing fiber fracture, but it can also create a temporary state that is not desirable for final bonding [N4-F3].

The practical implications for temperature, moisture, and pressure settings are clear. Moisture must be controlled precisely around dewpoint to avoid over-drying, which can damage mechanical properties [N3-R3]. Temperature should be balanced between densification and mechanical damage; the evidence shows that 90°C is more balanced than higher temperatures, while 240°C can reduce bending strength [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Pressure should be sufficient to keep the veneer together during pressing, but excessive pressure can be counteracted by the strength of ray structures and other natural reinforcements [N3-R5]. The broader evidence also suggests that softening and pressing are sensitive to the prior thermal and moisture history of the wood, because thermal pretreatments alter cellulose crystallinity and stress distribution [N2-F2]. Lignin’s role in softening is first determined by its molecular structure and thermal behavior. Its high Tg is largely explained by hydrogen bonding between phenolic hydroxyl groups and the higher quantity of aromatic rings in its main chain [N1-F1]. These features make lignin more rigid and thermally stable than many synthetic polymers, but also mean that softening occurs only when thermal energy disrupts these bonds and the aromatic architecture [N1-F1]. 

The same evidence also notes that lignin’s Tg lies between 100 and 180°C and that values obtained in the study are higher than some literature values for kraft lignin, partly because of its more condensed structure [N1-F1]. This means that lignin’s Tg is not a fixed number but is sensitive to source and isolation method. In other words, lignin’s thermal behavior must be interpreted in context: softening is not a simple threshold effect, but one that depends on the lignin’s specific chemistry [N1-F1].

---

## 2. Thermal and mechanical changes near lignin’s Tg in lignin-rich wood

Near lignin’s Tg, the wood behaves more plastically because the aromatic matrix is temporarily relaxed. The evidence on wood working processes states that when heat and moisture are applied, lignin softens temporarily, allowing wood fibers to slide instead of breaking [N4-F3]. It also notes that moisture makes wood more bendable, along with heat, and that lignin softening is central to this behavior [N4-R4]. This suggests that near Tg, lignin-rich wood becomes temporarily pliable rather than permanently degraded. 

At the same time, the evidence indicates that lignin decomposes in a wider temperature range (423–1173 K) than hemicellulose (493–588 K) and cellulose (588–673 K) [N2-R2]. This means that lignin’s thermal stability is broader than those of the other components, but softening is not just a matter of thermal decomposition; it is also about temporary plasticity. The wood-cell-wall context adds that cellulose microfibrils bear the primary load, while lignin dissipates stress under compression [N2-F2]. This is important because it shows that lignin’s role is not simply to resist heat; it also helps redistribute stress and enable temporary deformation [N2-F2].

Lignin’s Tg is distinct from that of cellulose and hemicellulose because the three components have different thermal and mechanical roles.
